analysis.one_liner: Phases out feeding medically important antibiotics to farm animals for growth promotion, to slow drug-resistant infections.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced by Sen. Edward Kennedy with 18 cosponsors, was referred to the Senate Health Committee and never advanced—no committee action, no vote, no debate—before the 111th Congress ended on January 3, 2011.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required the FDA to stop approving, and to withdraw approval of, using medically important antibiotics in healthy food animals for growth promotion and routine disease prevention, unless manufacturers proved the practice would not harm human health by breeding antibiotic-resistant bacteria. Under the bill, most such nontherapeutic uses would have been phased out within two years. It never received a hearing or a vote in the Senate committee it was sent to.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary people who rely on antibiotics to treat infections: pneumonia, food poisoning, scarlet fever, and other common illnesses. The bill aimed to keep these drugs working by removing the largest single driver of antibiotic resistance—the routine feeding of medically important antibiotics to healthy farm animals, which the bill's findings say accounts for roughly 70 percent of U.S. antibiotic use. Sick animals would still be treatable; doctors would keep effective drugs longer.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Everyone who might need an antibiotic

how_it_helps.text: Bars FDA approval of new animal drugs containing medically important antibiotics unless manufacturers prove a reasonable certainty of no harm to human health from resistance.

Directs FDA to withdraw approval of existing nontherapeutic uses of those drugs in food-producing animals within two years unless manufacturers demonstrate the same safety standard, while preserving legitimate uses to treat sick animals.

The bill's findings cite an estimated 70 percent of U.S. antibiotics going to farm animals without prescriptions, National Academy of Sciences estimates of $4–5 billion in annual public costs from resistant bacteria, and documented links between animal antibiotic use and resistant Salmonella, Campylobacter, and E. coli infections in people.

analysis.who_pays: Livestock producers and animal-drug manufacturers, who would lose routine antibiotics that compensate for crowded, unsanitary conditions and promote growth; some cost may pass to consumers as slightly higher meat prices.

drawbacks.text: The bill imposes a 2-year deadline for withdrawing approvals of nontherapeutic uses, which livestock producers and their veterinary advisors argued could raise production costs, particularly for large confinement operations that rely on routine antibiotics to compensate for crowded conditions.

An honest supporter would acknowledge that FDA would bear a heavy burden to conduct the risk analyses that determine which drugs keep their approvals, and that the bill's burden of proof on manufacturers is far stricter than the approval standard that existed when most of these antibiotics were originally cleared.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is large and durable: preserving antibiotic effectiveness protects everyone's ability to treat infections, at potentially modest consumer food-price increases. The cost falls on a concentrated industry rather than the public broadly. The main design objection—that livestock producers may rely on routine antibiotics in ways that are hard to replace quickly—is mitigated by the bill's two-year phase-out, its preservation of legitimate disease-prevention and treatment uses, and the safety-demonstration escape valve.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee on the day it was introduced, and the committee never took it up, so it died without a vote when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced in the Senate on March 17, 2009 and read twice before being referred to the Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee—its only action of the Congress.
The action history shows no hearing, no markup, no committee report, and no floor vote; the bill's last recorded action is the referral.
When the 111th Congress ended on January 3, 2011, the bill expired with it, leaving the approvals of medically important antibiotics for nontherapeutic farm use in place.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The meat and animal-drug industries, which kept unrestricted access to routine antibiotics in feed, are better off; the public keeps bearing the estimated $4–5 billion annual cost of resistant infections. Readers should also note the bill lacked a single Republican cosponsor.

for.name: Sen. Edward M. Kennedy
for.role: U.S. Senator (D-MA), bill sponsor and Chairman of the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill; it was referred to the committee he chaired, which nonetheless never acted on it during the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had bipartisan sponsorship (14 of 58 Democrats, 2 of 40 Republicans, and both independents cosponsored), but no vote ever occurred, so the partisan shape of the opposition is unknown.

industries.note: Producers would lose the ability to use medically important antibiotics routinely in feed and water for growth promotion and to compensate for crowded conditions, forcing changes in husbandry practices. Costs could show up as modestly higher meat prices.
Pharmaceutical companies selling feed-grade antibiotics would lose a major, largely prescription-free market segment unless they could prove safety under a stricter standard.
Doctors, hospitals, and patients gain longer-lasting antibiotic effectiveness, avoiding the expensive and sometimes failed treatment of resistant infections.
